title: Old regulatory DNA with no conserved base in mouse or human loses more diversity in wild mouse subspecies with larger population size; this fits weak selection but is confounded with subspecies
abstract: In wild house mice, old (alignable) candidate regulatory elements with no conserved base in mouse or human alignments lose more diversity, relative to nearby DNA, in subspecies with larger long-term population size. The direction fits weak purifying selection, but size is confounded with subspecies. This matters because human data show no selection on non-conserved regulatory DNA, and it was not known if the cause is no function or a human population too small for weak selection to act (the drift barrier). We measured nucleotide diversity (the mean difference between two genome copies) in ENCODE candidate regulatory elements (cCREs) in 7 wild mouse populations and in African-ancestry gnomAD genomes (chromosomes 19-22), against matched background DNA. Of mouse cCREs that the mouse alignment calls non-conserved but that align to human, 69% contain at least one base of a human 100- or 470-species conserved element (median 7 bp); these lose 7-15% of diversity. In strictly non-conserved old sequence (12 Mb), the loss relative to flanking DNA was 3.9%, 7.0% and 10.8% in musculus, domesticus and castaneus populations with long-term effective size 1.9, 2.5 and 5.0 x 10^5 (all SNVs). It grew by 3.8 points (95% CI 2.9-4.8) from domesticus to castaneus and by 3.1 (1.5-4.5) from musculus to domesticus, and was positive in all four combinations of site base and variant type; with GC-conservative variants (A<->T, C<->G) a net loss was seen only in castaneus (4.5%). Rodent-specific sequence showed less (0.4 points with GC-conservative variants). The evidence is not clean: the two contrasts do not fit one nearly-neutral curve, so effects not due to population size of 2-4 points exist; contrasts between ancestral and recently bottlenecked populations within subspecies were null for this class; composition offsets differ between populations; and segregating-site and singleton patterns did not separate selection from other causes. If the increase is selection, it corresponds to about 2-8 x 10^-7 per base, which predicts a 0.4-1.4% loss at human size; the human estimate (0.9%, 95% CI -4.2 to 6.1%) cannot test this. Limitations: subspecies and, for castaneus, sequencing batch are confounded with size; the human data cover 4 chromosomes; the strict class depends on short conserved elements.

display.caption: Diversity reduction D (1 - observed/expected) against effective population size N. A: conserved cCRE bases (blue), cCREs non-conserved in the mouse but conserved in the human alignment (orange), strictly non-conserved cCREs (aqua). B: strictly non-conserved old (orange) and lineage-specific (aqua) sequence and the 0.3-3 kb flanks of the old elements (gray). Filled circles: ancestral-range mouse populations; open circles: recently bottlenecked populations; diamonds: human (gnomAD African, chr19-22).

Diversity reduction by site base (A/T or G/C) and variant type in the three ancestral-range mouse populations (lines) and humans (diamonds). Levels differ between panels (composition offsets), but strictly non-conserved old cCRE sequence (orange) increases with N in all four; its flanks (gray) do not.

Differences in diversity reduction between ancestral-range populations with 95% bootstrap intervals: castaneus minus domesticus Iran (N x 2.0, dark) and domesticus Iran minus musculus Afghanistan (N x 1.3, same sequencing study, gray), for all non-CpG SNVs (A) and GC-conservative SNVs (B).
